storylines.title: The juntas' war with JNIM and IS Sahel
storylines.force: Insurgency for control of the rural Sahel
storylines.origins: Jihadist groups seized northern Mali in 2012. JNIM formed in 2017 as a federation of al-Qa'ida-aligned groups, and IS Sahel split from al-Mourabitoun in 2015.
storylines.drivers: Weak state presence in rural areas, armed-group control of artisanal gold sites, and local grievances the groups exploit.
storylines.aims: JNIM aims to remove state and Western presence and govern under its version of Sharia (UK Home Office). The juntas aim to retake territory by force.
storylines.direction: Attacks have spread from Mali into Burkina Faso, western Niger and the borderlands of coastal states.
storylines.counter: National armies, Russian forces, and local militias recruited by the juntas.
storylines.stakes: Control of territory, roads and gold sites across three states.
storylines.unresolved: Whether the juntas' break with Western partners leaves them able to hold rural areas.

storylines.title: Russia replaces France and the UN
storylines.origins: Coups in Mali (2020-21), Burkina Faso (2022) and Niger (2023) brought juntas that expelled French forces and the UN mission. Wagner arrived in Mali in 2021.
storylines.drivers: Junta demand for regime protection and fighting support, and Moscow's interest in influence and mining access.
storylines.aims: Moscow presents Africa Corps as state-to-state help. The juntas want partners without conditions on governance.
storylines.direction: Wagner left Mali in June 2025 and Africa Corps, under the Russian defence ministry, took over.
storylines.counter: Former Western partners, ECOWAS, and armed groups that target Russian forces.
storylines.stakes: Who supplies security in the Sahel and on what terms.
storylines.unresolved: How Russian forces are paid, beyond the reported mining stakes.

whos.d: Russian defence-ministry force that replaced Wagner
Russian private military company, proscribed by the UK in 2023
Confederation of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger

storylines.title: State control of gold and uranium
storylines.origins: The juntas revised mining codes and moved against foreign operators after taking power.
storylines.drivers: Revenue needs, sovereignty politics, and the gold that also funds armed groups.
storylines.aims: Niamey and Bamako present control of mines as returning wealth to citizens.
storylines.direction: Niger nationalised SOMAIR in June 2025 and Mali began building a refinery with Russia's Yadran Group.
storylines.counter: Foreign operators such as Orano, which took Niger to arbitration.
storylines.stakes: Uranium and gold revenue, and who buys them.
storylines.unresolved: Who will buy and finance Niger's uranium.

whos.d: Russian partner in Mali's gold refinery

storylines.title: ISWAP's campaign against army outposts
storylines.force: Jihadist insurgency in the Lake Chad basin
storylines.origins: Boko Haram's insurgency began in north-east Nigeria in 2009. ISWAP split from it in 2015-16 and pledged to Islamic State.
storylines.drivers: Shrinking lake livelihoods, remote outposts that are easy to isolate, and lake islands that troops struggle to reach.
storylines.aims: ISWAP aims to hold territory and tax civilians, and it seizes weapons from overrun bases (ISS).
storylines.direction: ISS counted at least 15 ISWAP attacks on outposts in the first half of 2025.
storylines.counter: The armies of Nigeria, Cameroon, Chad and Niger.
storylines.stakes: Control of north-east Nigeria's countryside and the lake economy.
storylines.unresolved: Whether Nigeria's resettlement outposts can be defended.

whos.d: North-east Nigerian state at the centre of the insurgency

storylines.title: Chad's break with France
storylines.origins: France kept bases in Chad from independence until 2025.
storylines.drivers: Chadian sovereignty politics and the regional shift away from France.
storylines.aims: N'Djamena says ending the pact restores full sovereignty over its security choices.
storylines.direction: France handed over its last base in January 2025.

storylines.title: The SAF-RSF war for the state
storylines.force: Contest for control of the Sudanese state
storylines.origins: The army (SAF) and the RSF together removed Bashir in 2019 and the civilian transition partners in 2021. They then fell out over folding the RSF into the army, and war began in April 2023.
storylines.drivers: Rival claims to rule, gold revenue, and foreign arms supply.
storylines.aims: The SAF says it defends the state against a rebel militia. The RSF says it fights Bashir-era Islamists.
storylines.direction: The RSF said it captured the army headquarters in El Fasher in October 2025, and drone warfare has intensified.
storylines.counter: Each side's foreign suppliers sustain the other's resistance.
storylines.stakes: Who rules Sudan, and the lives of civilians in Darfur, Kordofan and Gezira.
storylines.unresolved: Whether either side's backers will stop supplying them.

whos.d: Sudanese Armed Forces, led by Abdel Fattah al-Burhan
Rapid Support Forces, led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo (Hemedti)
Accused by UN experts of supplying the RSF, which it denies

storylines.title: M23, Rwanda and the Kivus
storylines.force: Contest over eastern Congo's land and minerals
storylines.origins: M23 first rose in 2012, was defeated in 2013, and resumed fighting in late 2021.
storylines.drivers: Mineral revenue, Rwandan security claims about the FDLR, and weak Congolese state control.
storylines.aims: Kigali says it defends itself against the FDLR. Kinshasa calls M23 a Rwandan proxy that loots its minerals.
storylines.direction: M23 holds Goma, Bukavu and the Rubaya mines, while US-brokered agreements tie peace to mineral trade.
storylines.counter: Congo's army, allied militias, and US and Qatari mediation.
storylines.stakes: Territory, coltan revenue, and millions of displaced people.
storylines.unresolved: Whether Rwandan troops withdraw under the 2025 agreements.

whos.d: Rebel movement and its political alliance
Hutu militia with roots in the 1994 genocide

storylines.title: Touadéra's Russian-protected state
storylines.origins: Wagner arrived in 2018 as the CAR government faced rebel coalitions.
storylines.drivers: Government need for protection, Russian interest in mining and timber.
storylines.aims: Bangui credits Russian and Rwandan forces with security gains. Moscow wants Africa Corps to replace Wagner and higher payment.
storylines.direction: Touadéra won a third term in December 2025.
storylines.stakes: Control of mining zones and the government's survival.
storylines.unresolved: Who replaces Wagner and on what terms.

storylines.title: Ethiopia's quest for the sea and the Nile dispute
storylines.force: Ethiopia's search for sea access and water security
storylines.origins: Ethiopia lost its coastline when Eritrea became independent in 1993. It began the GERD dam in 2011.
storylines.drivers: A landlocked population of over 100 million and Egypt's dependence on the Nile.
storylines.aims: Addis calls sea access existential. Egypt calls the dam a threat to its water supply. Eritrea calls Ethiopia's push irredentism.
storylines.direction: GERD opened in September 2025 and rhetoric over Assab escalated through 2025.
storylines.counter: Eritrea, Egypt, and their security pact.
storylines.stakes: War risk between Ethiopia and Eritrea, and Nile water shares.
storylines.unresolved: Any agreement on Nile water or sea access.

whos.d: Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile

storylines.title: Somalia's war with al-Shabaab and Islamic State
storylines.origins: Al-Shabaab has fought the Somali government since 2007. Islamic State-Somalia operates in Puntland.
storylines.drivers: Clan politics, weak federal institutions, and taxation of trade by al-Shabaab.
storylines.aims: Al-Shabaab seeks an Islamic state in Somalia and has pledged to al-Qa'ida (UK Home Office).
storylines.direction: AFRICOM carried out 124 strikes in Somalia in 2025.
storylines.counter: Somali federal and regional forces, African Union troops, US air strikes.
storylines.unresolved: Whether federal forces can hold areas without foreign air support.

storylines.title: Sahel jihadism reaches the coast
storylines.force: Southward spread of the Sahel insurgency
storylines.origins: JNIM attacks in northern Benin and Togo grew from the early 2020s.
storylines.drivers: Border parks with little state presence and routes from Burkina Faso and Niger.
storylines.aims: JNIM aims to remove state presence from areas it operates in.
storylines.direction: Benin acknowledged 54 soldiers killed in April 2025.
storylines.unresolved: Cross-border cooperation with the Sahel juntas.

storylines.title: Cabo Delgado insurgency and the LNG project
storylines.origins: An Islamic State-linked insurgency began in Cabo Delgado in 2017.
storylines.drivers: Local grievances, and the gas zone's strategic value.
storylines.aims: Kigali presents its deployment as security help. TotalEnergies wants the LNG project secured.
storylines.direction: TotalEnergies lifted force majeure in October 2025.
storylines.counter: Mozambique's army and more than 4,000 Rwandan troops.
storylines.stakes: A $20bn LNG project and civilian safety.

whos.d: US-designated group active in Cabo Delgado

storylines.title: Libya's divided state and its foreign patrons
storylines.force: Rival governments in Tripoli and the east
storylines.origins: Libya split after 2014. Haftar's 2019 offensive on Tripoli was halted by Turkish intervention in 2020.
storylines.drivers: Oil revenue, foreign patrons, and armed groups tied to each side.
storylines.aims: Turkey says it backs the legitimate government. Russia uses eastern bases to supply the Sahel.
storylines.direction: Russian flights to eastern Libya rose in late 2024.
storylines.counter: UN mediation and each side's rivals.
storylines.stakes: Oil revenue and a supply corridor into the Sahel.
storylines.unresolved: Unification of the government and central bank.

storylines.title: Foreign powers compete for influence
storylines.force: Great-power and middle-power competition in Africa
storylines.origins: China, Russia, Gulf states, Turkey and Western powers have expanded diplomatic, financial and military ties.
storylines.drivers: Minerals, markets, votes in international forums, and security partnerships.
storylines.aims: Each power presents its role as partnership. See the backer lines on the map for documented actions.
storylines.direction: Summits and financing announcements continue across the continent.
storylines.counter: African governments playing partners against each other.
storylines.stakes: Who finances, arms and trades with African states.
storylines.unresolved: Debt terms and the conditions attached to new partnerships.
